title: Aquatic animals farmed in South Africa

lessons.title: Freshwater fish
lessons.html:
Fish that live in fresh water

Rainbow trout

  • Needs cold, clean water with lots of oxygen.
  • Farmed in the mountains of the Western Cape and Mpumalanga, in dams, tanks and raceways (long channels with running water).
  • Eats pellet feed with a lot of protein.
  • Trout is not from South Africa. It came from North America long ago. Farms need permits and must stop trout from escaping.

Tilapia

  • Likes warm water. It does not grow well in cold winters.
  • Farmed in ponds and tanks in warmer areas such as Limpopo and KwaZulu-Natal.
  • Eats plant-based pellet feed and is easy to farm.
  • The Mozambique tilapia is from southern Africa. Other kinds, like the Nile tilapia, are not local and need special permits.
  • Tilapia breed very quickly. Too many small fish can fill a pond.

African sharptooth catfish (barbel)

  • A local South African fish.
  • Very tough. It can live in water with little oxygen, because it can breathe air at the surface.
  • Grows fast in warm water.
  • Eats pellets and is farmed in tanks and ponds.
  • Handle with care: it has sharp spines on its fins.

Koi and other ornamental fish

Koi and goldfish are farmed for garden ponds, not for food. Buyers pay for colour and pattern, so they must be handled very gently.

lessons.title: Marine animals
lessons.html:
Animals from the sea

Abalone (perlemoen)

  • A big sea snail with one shell. It sticks to rocks.
  • Farmed in tanks on land with sea water pumped in, mostly in the Western Cape.
  • Eats seaweed (kelp) and special pellet feed.
  • Grows very slowly. It takes a few years to reach selling size.
  • Very valuable. Wild abalone is often poached, so farms have strong security.

Mussels

  • A shellfish with two shells.
  • Grown on ropes hanging from rafts in the sea, for example in Saldanha Bay.
  • Mussels filter tiny plants and particles from the water. They do not need to be fed.

Oysters

  • Also a shellfish with two shells.
  • Grown in baskets or racks in bays and lagoons, for example near Knysna and on the West Coast.
  • Also filter food from the water.

Marine fish

Some farms grow sea fish such as dusky kob in tanks. This is still a small part of the industry.

Seaweed

Seaweed is grown on some farms, sometimes to feed abalone.

Why filter feeders need clean water

Mussels and oysters eat what is in the water. If the water is polluted, or there is a harmful algae bloom (red tide), the shellfish can become poisonous to people. Farms must test them before selling. When there is a red tide warning, harvesting stops.

lessons.title: Comparing the animals
lessons.html:
Each animal needs different care

AnimalWaterTemperatureFood
TroutFreshColdHigh-protein pellets
TilapiaFreshWarmPellets
CatfishFreshWarmPellets
AbaloneSeaCoolSeaweed and pellets
MusselsSeaCoolFilter from water
OystersSeaCool to mildFilter from water

Why this matters to you

  • If you put trout in warm water, they get stressed and can die.
  • If tilapia get too cold in winter, they stop eating and can get sick.
  • If you overfeed fish, the leftover feed rots and makes the water bad.
  • Abalone need gentle handling. If they are pulled off the tank wall roughly, they can be hurt and bleed.

Signs of a healthy animal

  • Fish swim normally and come to eat at feeding time.
  • Fish have clean skin and fins with no sores.
  • Abalone stick firmly to the tank wall.
  • Shellfish close their shells when touched.

If animals are not eating, swimming at the surface gasping, or dying, tell your supervisor at once.

Key points

  • Trout need cold, clean water; tilapia and catfish like warm water.
  • Abalone grow slowly in sea water tanks and eat seaweed and pellets.
  • Mussels and oysters filter their food from the water.
  • Shellfish can become poisonous during a red tide, so harvesting stops.
  • Report fish that stop eating, gasp at the surface or die.
